newsitem.title: USA: L.A. politician offers "evidence" of CIA drug ties.
newsitem.headline: L.A. politician offers "evidence" of CIA drug ties.

text.p: A U.S. Congresswoman from a drug-infested area of Los Angeles said on Monday she has evidence the CIA helped sell crack cocaine in black neighbourhoods to fund right-wing Contra rebels in Nicaragua 10 years ago.

Democrat Maxine Waters said she had obtained records from the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department showing that law enforcement officials had failed to stop a man who claimed to work for the CIA from selling illegal drugs in south central Los Angeles in 1986.

Sheriff Sherman Block responded by saying that although it was no secret that huge quantities of cocaine were sold in the predominantly black area and proceeds were laundered in Florida and returned to Latin America, "there is nothing to indicate any knowledge or involvement by the CIA."
If the government spy agency had been involved in such activity, "then they should be dealt with in the same way as anyone else who stoops so low," Block told a news conference.
Last month the former head of the Contras, Adolfo Calero, told Reuters in Managua that the charge of CIA involvement in drug trafficking was "absurd."

Last week Sen. Dianne Feinstein, a California Democrat, urged the Senate to investigate whether the CIA had supported the sale of crack cocaine in Los Angeles in 1986 to help fund Contra rebels fighting the left-wing government of Nicaragua.
Feinstein urged leaders of the Senate Judiciary and Intelligence committees to hold joint hearings on the issue in the next Congress.

The San Jose Mercury News published a three-part series in August suggesting that the CIA had been involved in financing the Contra rebels fighting Nicaragua's Sandinista government through the smuggling of crack into poor neighbourhoods in Los Angeles and other cities in the 1980s.
The Justice Department is investigating the charges and the CIA is also conducting an internal investigation.

Waters, who is running for re-election, held a news conference at an intersection in south central Los Angeles near where Nicaraguan dealer Danilo Blandon allegedly sold up to 22 pounds (10 kg) of cocaine a week from a bar.
She produced photocopies of sheriff's department reports and affidavits that she said indicated law-enforcement authorities had been aware of a CIA connection during a series of raids in 1986.

Waters said one suspect, a former policeman in neighbouring Orange County who was seized by a special narcotics unit of the sheriff's deartment, told officers: "You can't arrest me. I work for the CIA."

He was allowed to call what he said was his contact at CIA headquarters in Langley, Virginia. The man, who Waters said had been responsible for first putting Uzis and AK-47s in the hands of south central drug dealers, was never convicted.
Waters said an affidavit from a man convicted in the drug raids had been sealed by a judge and its contents suppressed.
She said he had said under oath, "If evidence proves the government was involved (in drug distribution), that certainly would be my defence."
